items.prompt: In the recipe story, why did the cake fail a second time?
choices: Only one of three cards was corrected
The fixed card was copied wrongly again
The oven was set to the wrong heat
items.explanation: The fix reached one card. The other two still held the mistake.

items.prompt: When does the cost of a pasted copy usually show up?
choices: The moment the code is pasted
Only when the file itself is finally deleted
When the logic later has to be changed
items.explanation: Pasting works immediately. The bill comes when every copy must be changed.

items.prompt: A bug is found in a rule pasted in 3 places. How many places contain the bug?
items.explanation: Each pasted copy carries its own instance of the same bug.

items.prompt: You fix the bug in 1 of 3 copies. How many copies still have it?
items.explanation: Fixing one copy leaves the other two untouched.

items.prompt: What does DRY stand for?
choices: Do Review Yearly
Debug Rapidly Yourself
Don't Repeat Yourself
items.explanation: DRY is the rule that each piece of knowledge has a single home.

items.prompt: What is the main goal of DRY?
choices: Each function is kept very short
A change to a rule happens in only one place
No two files in the project may ever look alike
items.explanation: With one home for the rule, one edit updates everything that uses it.

items.prompt: Why is a forgotten copy especially dangerous?
choices: Nobody knows to fix it, so the bug returns
It makes the whole program run noticeably slower
It is always the largest copy in the whole project
items.explanation: A copy nobody remembers never gets the fix.

items.prompt: Why does pasting feel harmless?
choices: Copies are checked by the compiler
Pasted code never contains bugs
The pasted copy works right away
items.explanation: The cost is deferred, so it is easy to ignore.

items.prompt: The same rounding rule is pasted in checkout, the cart preview and an admin tool. A fix lands in checkout and is released. What is the most likely next event?
choices: The admin tool fails to compile after the release
A near-identical bug report from the cart preview
Checkout rejects the fix because of the copies
All three places update when the build runs
items.explanation: Nothing connects the copies, so only the edited one changes. The other two still hold the old bug.
items.reference:
The bill arrives at change time
📇 paste: instant, works immediately
🔧 change: every copy must be found and fixed
👻 a forgotten copy: same bug reported again
Why: one bug in three copies needs three fixes, and the one nobody remembers gets missed.
items.learnMore:
What copy-paste really costs

Pasting is cheap now and expensive later. Each copy is an independent place the same fact lives, so every future change multiplies by the number of copies, and the forgotten ones keep the old bug alive.

Common mistake

Thinking a bug was fixed because it was fixed once. It was fixed in one copy only.

A fifth copy that nobody remembers keeps the bug
The fixes only work if made in the original
items.explanation: Fixing every known copy is not the same as fixing every copy. Unknown copies are the real risk.

items.prompt: Two pieces of code express the same rule and must always change together. What kind of duplication is this?
choices: Coincidental duplication
True duplication of one rule
Premature abstraction of a rule
items.explanation: One rule repeated is exactly what DRY targets.

items.prompt: Two pieces of code look alike but exist for different reasons. What is this called?
choices: Coincidental duplication
True duplication
A shared constant between modules
items.explanation: They match by chance today and will change independently.

items.prompt: What should you do with true duplication?
choices: Leave all the copies in place
Delete one copy and hope the rest still work
Extract one shared function
items.explanation: One rule should have one home.

items.prompt: What should you do with coincidental duplication?
choices: Merge them into one
Leave the pieces separate
Copy them to a third place
items.explanation: Merging look-alikes ties unrelated rules together.

items.prompt: The cake and casserole cards both say 'bake 30 minutes'. Should they be merged into one card?
choices: No, they are separate rules
Yes, the text is identical
Yes, to save paper and space in the drawer
items.explanation: If the cake time changes, the casserole should not.

items.prompt: What is premature abstraction?
choices: Writing code before the design has been formally approved by the team
Naming a function before you have actually written its body
Extracting a shared function before the duplication is proven
items.explanation: Abstracting too early guesses at a rule that may not exist.

items.prompt: What can a premature abstraction end up being?
choices: Always shorter and clearer
More tangled than the copies it replaced
Impossible to compile in most languages today
items.explanation: A forced shared function often needs branches to serve both callers.

items.prompt: Which question separates the two kinds of duplication?
choices: Do they change for the same reason?
Are they the same length?
Were they both written on the same day?
items.explanation: Same reason to change means same rule.

items.prompt: A tax function and a discount function both multiply by a percentage and round to cents. Which action best fits DRY?
choices: Keep them separate unless one rule governs both
Merge them, because the arithmetic is identical in both cases
Delete the discount function and reuse the tax logic instead
Merge them behind a flag that selects which one to run
items.explanation: They are two rules that share a shape, so they are likely to diverge.
items.reference:
Same look is not same rule
🍰 cake: bake 30 minutes
🍲 casserole: bake 30 minutes
cake changes to 35: casserole must stay at 30
→ coincidental duplication: do not merge
Why: merge only copies of one rule that must always change together.

True duplication repeats one rule, so it should be merged. Coincidental duplication repeats a shape, so merging it ties together things that will diverge.

Common mistake

Judging by how similar the code looks instead of whether the rules change together.

Delete one of them and see what breaks
Leave them separate for now

items.prompt: Where does the second change go when merged rules diverge?
choices: Nowhere, the change vanishes
Inside the shared function

Yes, if they encode the same rule

items.explanation: Writing one rule in two shapes still repeats the rule.

items.prompt: Two functions are byte-for-byte identical. A teammate wants to merge them. What is the strongest question to ask first?
choices: Which of the two functions was written first by the team?
Can the merged version stay under fifty lines in total?
Do both of the functions already have unit tests?
Would one business rule change both at once?
items.explanation: Identical text is weak evidence. A shared reason to change is what justifies a merge.
items.reference:
The test
Would a change to the rule need to hit both places?
✅ always → true duplication → extract
❓ not always, or unsure → coincidental → leave separate
merged look-alikes: the second change moves inside the shared function
Why: DRY asks whether the rules are the same, not whether the text matches.
items.learnMore:
The same-reason-to-change test

Ask what would cause each piece of code to change. If one business rule drives both, they belong together. If different rules drive them, a shared function only postpones the split and makes it harder.

Common mistake

Assuming identical code today means identical code tomorrow.

items.prompt: According to the rule of three, when do you extract a shared function?
choices: On the third occurrence
On the very first copy you write
Never, because copies are always fine
items.explanation: By then there is enough evidence of a real pattern.

items.prompt: What should you do the first time you write something?
choices: Abstract it at once
Copy it twice first
Just write it
items.explanation: A single instance has nothing to be duplicated against.

items.prompt: What should you usually do at the second occurrence?
choices: Leave it, but take note of it
Extract a shared function
Rewrite both from scratch
items.explanation: Two cases are not enough to tell true from coincidental duplication.

items.prompt: Why is a third occurrence more useful than a second?
choices: It shows what varies between cases
It makes the code run faster
It proves the first two were wrong
items.explanation: Three cases make the constant part and the varying part visible.

items.prompt: Is the rule of three a law of nature?
choices: Yes, it is an exact mathematical law
Yes, but only in strongly typed languages
No, it is a practical heuristic
items.explanation: It stands in for 'enough evidence', which can vary.

items.prompt: What is the risk of extracting after one occurrence?
choices: Writing far too many tests for it
Guessing an abstraction with no evidence
Using noticeably less memory than needed
items.explanation: With one case the shape of the abstraction is pure guesswork.

items.prompt: After extracting on the third copy, what is the abstraction based on?
choices: Real cases, not a guess
A prediction of what future callers might need
The longest of the copies
items.explanation: Three real instances show what is constant.

items.prompt: What does 'take note' at two occurrences mean?
choices: Delete one of the two copies right away to be tidy
Add a comment saying that nobody should ever touch it
Remember the duplication so a third triggers action
items.explanation: You are watching for the third case that settles the question.

items.prompt: A pattern has appeared twice. A colleague proposes a shared helper now. What is the best response based on the rule of three?
choices: Agree, because two copies are always enough to extract
Delete one copy and keep only the other one
Wait: two cases cannot show what actually varies
Agree, because helpers are very cheap to remove later
items.explanation: With two cases the boundary of the abstraction is still a guess.
items.reference:
Evidence builds with each copy
1️⃣ one copy: nothing to compare
2️⃣ two copies: could be a rule or a coincidence
3️⃣ three copies: shared shape and variation visible
→ extract on the third, not before
Why: a third case shows what is really constant and what varies.
items.learnMore:
The rule of three

Tolerate duplication the first two times, and extract on the third. The point is evidence: with only two cases you are guessing where the abstraction's edge should be.

Common mistake

Treating three as a law. It is a proxy for having enough evidence, not a number to obey blindly.
items.reflection: Think of a task you repeat. How many times did you do it before you were confident which parts never change?

items.prompt: What is the warning sign of an abstraction extracted too early?
choices: A function with a very short name
A flag parameter that switches between two callers' behavior
A file with only one function
items.explanation: The flag stitches together two rules that never shared one.

items.prompt: calculateDiscount(price, qty, isBulk) branches on isBulk. What does that suggest?

One rule with a harmless variation
A performance optimization
items.explanation: The flag chooses which rule to run.

items.prompt: Who has to understand both branches of a flagged function?
choices: Only the original author
Nobody, since the flag hides the branches

items.explanation: To use either branch safely you need to know the other exists.

items.prompt: Is every boolean parameter automatically a forced abstraction?

No, it is a prompt to check
Yes, if it is named is something
items.explanation: A flag can be a narrow variation on one real rule.

items.prompt: What would turn formatPrice(amount, isRefund) into a real warning sign?

Adding a comment above it
Renaming the function
items.explanation: Diverging needs are the sign that two rules were joined.

items.prompt: A flag is acceptable when the two cases are...

Owned by different teams
One rule with a small variation
items.explanation: If nothing else ever differs, the flag is narrow.

items.prompt: What does a forced abstraction usually do to later changes?
choices: Make them impossible to test
Make them harder
Make them disappear
items.explanation: Each change must avoid breaking both callers.

items.prompt: What should you do on spotting such a flag?
choices: Ask if the branches are really one rule or two
Remove the flag without looking
Add a second flag
items.explanation: The fix depends on the answer to that question.

items.prompt: A function gains a fourth boolean parameter to support yet another caller. What is the most accurate diagnosis?
choices: The function is now well abstracted and needs no more care

Only the calling code is the real source of the problem
Booleans are forbidden outright by the DRY principle itself
items.explanation: Each new flag adds a rule behind one signature.

The warning sign
calculateDiscount(price, qty, isBulk)
isBulk exists only to switch between two callers
→ two rules joined by an if, not one rule with a variation
every future caller must understand both branches
Why: a flag that picks between callers marks rules stitched together too early.
items.learnMore:
The boolean flag warning sign

When a parameter exists only so a function can serve two callers differently, ask whether those callers share a rule. The flag is a prompt to check, not an automatic verdict.

Common mistake

Assuming every flag is a design failure, or that no flag ever is. Check whether the branches are really one rule.

items.reference:
The warning sign
calculateDiscount(price, qty, isBulk)
isBulk exists only to switch between two callers
→ two rules joined by an if, not one rule with a variation
every future caller must understand both branches
Why: a flag that picks between callers marks rules stitched together too early.
items.learnMore:
The boolean flag warning sign

When a parameter exists only so a function can serve two callers differently, ask whether those callers share a rule. The flag is a prompt to check, not an automatic verdict.

Common mistake

Assuming every flag is a design failure, or that no flag ever is. Check whether the branches are really one rule.
items.reflection: Think of a form, tool or process at work that has a 'special case' switch. Is it one process with a variation, or two processes sharing a screen?

items.prompt: In the case study, what total did the flagged function give for 5 units at $10 for a loyalty member?
items.explanation: The loyalty branch is checked first and applies 15% off.

items.prompt: Who decided that loyalty beats bulk in the flagged code?
choices: The product manager in a meeting
Nobody, branch order decided it
The customer
items.explanation: The if came before the else if.

items.prompt: Why were the old tests still green after the loyalty flag?
choices: None ran both rules on one call
They were deleted
They tested the loyalty rule
items.explanation: Overlap was a new case no test covered.

items.prompt: What is a hidden priority?
choices: A priority marked in the UI
A rule that is never used
A winner decided by code order, not by a stated choice
items.explanation: It was never written down as a decision.

items.prompt: Which total would stacking both discounts give (5 units at $10)?
items.explanation: 50 times 0.85 times 0.9 is 38.25.

items.prompt: What does a passing test suite prove?
choices: Cases someone wrote still work
Every possible case is correct
The code needs no changes
items.explanation: Tests only cover what their authors thought of.

items.prompt: When do the bulk and loyalty rules overlap?
choices: Any customer buying 1 unit
Non-members buying 3 units
Loyalty member buying 5 or more
items.explanation: Loyalty starts at 3 and bulk at 5, so 5 or more with membership matches both.

items.prompt: Why is a silent overlap bug risky?
choices: It crashes the whole shop
It returns a plausible number with no error
It always gives zero
items.explanation: Nothing signals that a decision was made.

items.prompt: After the loyalty flag is added, a loyalty member buys 5 units at $10 and pays $42.50. Which statement is accurate?
choices: Loyalty beat bulk because of branch order, not a decision
The two discounts correctly stacked together to give $42.50
Bulk beat loyalty and so the total is the correct one
The function crashed and quietly fell back to a default
items.explanation: Only one rule applied, and the winner came from which if was written first.
items.reference:
5 units at $10, loyalty member
bulk alone (10% off): $45
loyalty alone (15% off): $42.50
both stack: $38.25
the flagged code returned $42.50 without anyone choosing
Why: when two rules overlap, the winner must be a stated decision, not the order of two if-branches.
items.learnMore:
Hidden priority

Adding a rule behind a flag makes the code's branch order silently decide which rule wins. Old tests never exercise the overlap, so the decision ships unreviewed.

Common mistake

Concluding the code is right because every earlier test still passes.
items.reflection: Think of two policies that can both apply to the same case at your workplace. Who decides which one wins, and is it written down?

items.prompt: Which test would have exposed the priority problem?
choices: A non-member buying 5 units
A loyalty member buying exactly 5 units
A non-member buying 2 units
A loyalty member buying 1 unit
items.explanation: Only a call satisfying both rules reveals which one wins.

It breaks every existing caller immediately
It lets rules overlap without anyone stating a priority
It prevents any new tests from being written

The flagged result of $42.50 is a bug in math
The overlap can only be resolved by the customer
There were three defensible answers, not one

items.prompt: What changed numerically between the flag version and the ordered-rules version?
choices: Nothing changed
Every total
Only the bulk totals
items.explanation: The refactor made priority visible without changing results.

items.prompt: In the ordered-rules version, what states the priority?
choices: A comment above the function
The name of the function
The order of the rules in the list
items.explanation: The first matching rule wins.

items.prompt: How do you add a third discount rule?
choices: Add another nested if to every rule
Add one more entry to the list
Rewrite the whole function
items.explanation: Rules are independent entries.

items.prompt: Which rule is checked first in the fix?
choices: Loyalty
Bulk
A random one
items.explanation: Loyalty is listed before bulk.

items.prompt: What is the purpose of the ordered-rules refactor?
choices: Make totals smaller
Remove the loyalty rule
Make the priority explicit
items.explanation: The decision is now written down in the structure.

items.prompt: For quantity 2 and no loyalty, which total does the fixed version give at $10 each?
items.explanation: No rule applies, so the full total stands.

items.prompt: For 3 units at $10 as a loyalty member, what is the total?
Does the fix change which rule wins for a loyalty member buying 5 units?
choices: Yes, bulk now wins
Yes, both now stack
No, loyalty still wins, but now explicitly
items.explanation: The behavior was kept; only its visibility changed.

items.prompt: A business owner decides bulk should beat loyalty. What is the smallest change to the ordered-rules version?
choices: Add a flag to the shared function
Rewrite every caller of the function
Delete the loyalty rule from the list
Swap the order of the two entries
items.explanation: Priority is carried by list order, so reordering states the new decision.
items.reference:
Ordered rules
1. loyalty: member and quantity 3 or more → 0.85
2. bulk: quantity 5 or more → 0.90
first rule that applies wins
new rule = one more entry in the list
Why: the list order is the written statement of priority, so it can be reviewed and changed.
items.learnMore:
Composition instead of a flag

Express each rule as its own entry and let the order of the list state which wins. Results are unchanged from the flag version, but the decision is now visible.

Common mistake

Expecting the refactor to change totals. It changes legibility, not behavior.
items.reflection: Think of a decision at work made by 'whichever check happens first'. How could you make that order explicit and reviewable?

items.prompt: Which is the main benefit of the ordered-rules form over the flag form?
choices: Priority is visible and changeable in one place
It makes every discount larger
It removes the need for any tests
It runs a different rule per customer at random
items.explanation: The decision is stated rather than hidden in branch order.
